utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, sorry about that. Could you please call the case, and good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. And also good afternoon to my learned friend of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you and your team. So I asked the staff to convey to the witness -- to inform the witness that we would -- that he would come in with some delay so that in the meantime we deal with some of the issues that we have pending. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 2.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't forget, Madam Registrar, that this witness is testifying with one protective measure. Incidentally, just for the record because we have been in private session almost since the beginning of this sitting, we also had to stop for some time because there was a technical problem which has now been solved. And I thank the technicians for that. Supposedly, I think, you have been informed that today's schedule is adapted according to everybody's wish in a way that there will be only one break of 30 minutes at 4.00. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had enough time to relax over the long weekend that you have been here with us in The Hague. The weather has also been favourable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will continue and finish with your testimony today. Before we do so I want to put your mind at rest that we are starting now with your testimony because we needed to discuss a few preliminary matters amongst ourselves that have got nothing to do with you; they are preliminary matters relating to the case but they needed to be decided or discussed today. And then in addition we had some technical problems, and therefore we couldn't start immediately after we finished discussing the preliminary matters. You are testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made last week; it still applies today. You don't need to make it again or repeat it. Ms. Richardson is going to proceed and finish with her cross-examination, and then there will be a short re-examination by the Defence and then some questions from us and you will be able to go back home. Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'd like to continue from where we left off last Wednesday, and time is of the essence today so I would appreciate it if you can assist me by answering yes and no wherever possible to my questions. And if you desire to give a more detailed explanation, then that of course will be provided to you, but first of all I'd like to ask you to be as brief as possible and where possible give me yes or no answer. I'd like to ask you a question about the women -- the Muslim women specifically during the period of the war in 1992. Did any of the women -- were they ever considered fighters or did they participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the fighting, but they helped the fighters. They would wash their laundry, that sort of thing, but they were not involved in the fighting itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Would they also administer medical attention when necessary?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one of them knew how to do it, probably they would have helped out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this assistance that was rendered to the fighters was done wherever the fighters happened to be located, whether it was in Cizmici or in the wider area of Glogova, wherever the fighters happened to be?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the most part, they were around Cizmici. So the fighters would go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were Muslim women -- I'll rephrase the question. Do you discount the possibility that women -- Muslim women wore military uniform and engaged in the fighting during 1992 to mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discount that possibility. They did not carry weapons. I never saw any of them carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry, you didn't see any of them but there's a possibility that this could have happened but you just don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because your question and his answer do not tally. I mean -- yes, Ms. Vidovic. The question was about uniforms and engaged in fighting, and the answer was that they did not carry weapons, never saw any one of them carrying weapons. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason is the Prosecutor asked a very broad and imprecise question. The question was whether the witness could discount the possibility that during the fighting in 1992 and 1993 women who were fighters were wearing uniform, but what they should do is specify both time and place. They can't simply go and ask the witness whether in a very general sense the witness was aware of the Muslim women wearing uniform. Is this in reference to Glogova? Glogova, Tuzla, Sarajevo, which specific location do they have in mind? The question is highly imprecise and that's why the witness is providing this sort of answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure on redirect Madam Vidovic can ask for a further clarification. I'm simply asking a general question about his knowledge of women during 1992 and 1993, nothing more. And I am not going to specify any further; it's just a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can leave it at that, actually, I mean, and he has already answered that his knowledge he is not aware of any women fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know a Fatima Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fatima Golic, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anyone from your village of Glogova by the name of Fatima?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our village there were at least 15 to 20 ladies named Fatima, but none of them called Golic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a common Muslim name, Fatima.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Evidently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And -- thank you, sir. I'll move on to my next question. Now, last Wednesday you were discussing or testifying about the Glogova attack. Do you recall that? And I'm specifically referring to the attack that took place on the 23rd and the 24th of December, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the strategic importance was of Glogova? And when I say "strategic importance" I mean the importance to -- the importance of that area to both the Muslim fighters as well as the Serb soldiers or the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a group of fighters that we had at Glogova. There were people there, too; they were inside Glogova and they were surrounded. We went there to help them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. My question, though, is: Was Glogova important in terms of its location, important enough that the Muslims would seek to -- would seek to go in and liberate it or take control of that area?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our village --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In addition to --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was always important to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that it was your village, however, would you say that Glogova was important in terms of its location, and that being that it was located strategically between Kravica and Bratunac? Would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question, what exactly it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically -- let me phrase the question myself. Of course, sir, I do fully understand your answer, your response to Madam Richardson's question when you said, "of course we fought to take it back, it's our own village." But apart from that, apart from the fact that this was your village and you wanted to take it back, was there also the strategic aspect that influenced your decision to fight and take back Glogova? Was it important for you to take back only because it was our village or also because it was strategically important for the Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cizmici is a very small village, and yet there were between 1.000 and 1.500 civilians there. I'm talking about the area between Cizmici and Glogova. It was really crowded. There were lots of people there, and people could no longer continue to live in Cizmici. It's a very small area, so that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't know if you want to pursue this any further, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed. Perhaps the witness could be given Defence Exhibit 793, the map, and maybe we can have the map assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at Defence Exhibit D793, could you -- could you tell us -- could you point to where Glogova is just with the pointer? You don't have to mark it; it's already marked by you last week.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Velika Glogova is not on this map and there are a number of other villages that are not shown on this map. It's just Glogova. That's all it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had this -- 797, please, D797. And could the technician focus on the area which is marked in red and in green, please. Lower right -- oh, I see, I see, these are -- lower right. Yes, that's it. Yes, and if we could focus. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the area of Glogova, or the wider area I should say, that area is located, is it not, between Bratunac and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question to you is: During the time -- I'll rephrase the question. In December of 1992, on the 23rd and the 24th, prior to this time, prior to the time that Glogova was liberated by the Muslim forces, could you tell us whether it was in the hands of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kicked us out on the 24th of August. They drove us out of Glogova. In late summer and early autumn, another group entered Glogova and it was in Glogova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So during that period of time the Serbs had it. Now, you were just testifying -- you said it was important that your village was recaptured by you, at least it was important for the people of Glogova. But my question is: With respect to the military purpose of -- of Glogova, the area itself, once the Muslim forces managed to seize the area of Glogova on the 23rd and the 24th of December, did this not effectively mean that the Serbs from Bratunac and Kravica could no longer communicate? In other words, Glogova was the line of communication for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- or rather, their patrols controlled the road at the time. The people at Glogova and Vares were surrounded, and all the other villages I've mentioned. People where there from the right looking to the direction of Bratunac. People were surrounded. Looking from Bratunac to Kravica to the right, Muslims in those areas were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So it was important to the Muslims to re-take Glogova, other than the fact that it was your village and you had, of course, a vested interest in going back there?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, we already had people there who were nearly surrounded. We had to go and help them, otherwise they would all have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, that it was important to the Muslims to re-take Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we had to go and defend our people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And having re-taken Glogova on the 24th of December, did this not effectively result in the Serbs of Bratunac being unable to communicate with the Serbs in Kravica? In other words, breaking their line of communication.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection. All the while the witness has been answering questions by the Prosecutor, saying that part of the Muslims were surrounded in Glogova. And he keeps saying part of the Muslims were in Glogova. And the Prosecutor persists in claiming that the witness -- or putting it to the witness that they re-took Glogova, thus continually confusing the witness. Please, Witness, tell me: Are you not saying that you were in Glogova the whole time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm saying. I'm saying that to the right of the road --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, you have a right to object, of course, but you don't have a right then to go straight to the witness and ask him a question. Let the Trial Chamber do that. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think at this point you can raise this matter on re-examination if you want. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible for the decision to attack Glogova or, excuse me, re-capture Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. Who specifically do you mean who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I can rephrase that. There was a decision made to go in to Glogova on the 23rd and the 24th and to attack or counter-attack the Serb forces, was there not?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, meaning we wanted to go and help those people on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who made the decision to go help these people?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, Ejub came out in front of a group of people in Cizmici and explained to them that there were people who were surrounded. He asked whether we should go and help them or whether we should just allow them all to be killed. Of course our decision was to go and help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified as far as you know -- well, I'll rephrase that question. You testified last Wednesday that other than the men who fought under Ejub Golic, there were no other fighters from any other areas involved in this attack. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one, with the exception of Cizmici. I mean, the people of Cizmici; no one else was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the people of Cizmici made up one of the four groups you've testified was led by Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in that group, that particular group that was at Cizmici. Cizmici is a small village. There weren't that many of them, perhaps as many as 15 or 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did Ejub Golic get the men together, the 400 approximate men, that made up part of your group and did he decide what direction they would all go in?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never mentioned how many. There was one large group at Glogova, but I never said anything about the one at Cizmici. I don't know, therefore I can't specify. There were no documents that were kept, and I don't know how many men that group comprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, you testified last Wednesday that there were approximately 400 men -- this is collectively of all the four groups, approximately?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the total of four groups that were there. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, there were groups, but I don't know about each and every one of them. You kept asking me to give you a number, but I simply don't know this number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, you still don't know how many men were in the groups you participated in when you entered Glogova on the 23rd and 24th?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you don't know if it were 50 men or a hundred men. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know the exact number. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, did Ejub Golic mention that re-taking Glogova would give the Muslim forces a strategic advantage, in that it would cut off the communication lines between the Serbs in Kravica and the Serbs in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. I told you there were people there. A group of men were at Glogova, and the civilians were already there. Once they were surrounded, we just went there to help them; that was the main objective we had, to help the people who were at Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you do maintain, do you not, that the Serbs from Kravica was getting assistance from the Serbs in Bratunac during that period of time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which specific date do you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In 1992, from May to December, up until the time that the Glogova counter-attack took place, you maintain, do you not, that the Serbs from Kravica and Jezestica were getting assistance from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so, if you were to re-take Glogova it doesn't -- does it not stand to reason that the Serbs in Kravica and Bratunac would no longer be able to communicate?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took the road near Glogova and they had another road to use, the one from Bratunac through Polom and on to Kravica. So the one you're referring to is not the only road being used by the Serbs in terms of using it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can assist us and point to your map where the -- what road you're referring to that the Serbs could use. And if that map isn't adequate, we can perhaps use the other map.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see Bratunac here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand. Perhaps D793 can assist you.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I show it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Bratunac here, and there's a road here along the river Drina, Slapasnica, Krasno Polje, as far as Polom, and you can go along this road and then they could go from Polom to Kravica. They could use that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, you would admit, would you not, that that's a rather long way for the Serbs to get from Bratunac to Kravica than going through Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were we supposed to let them kill us all in Glogova so that they could go any way they wanted? I don't know what you're trying to say to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can answer my question and tell us: Based on what you've just indicated on the map whether the distance from Bratunac to Kravica, going the way that you pointed close to the Drina was significantly further than them going through Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had tanks. They had APCs. They had motor vehicles, and they could use that road. It wouldn't have been such a big problem for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So in other words -- so re-taking Glogova had no strategic purpose, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I've been trying to explain to you all this time that there were people on the right side of the road from Bratunac to Kravica. They were in Velika Glogova and Kravica and people were encircled and we went there to help those people. There's no other way I can explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not belabour this point any further, Ms. Richardson. Just ask the witness to explain again whether in his opinion it would have been easier for the Serbs to move from Bratunac to Kravica passing through Glogova than having to round the route that he explained to us before, even considering the fact that they had tanks and APCs and whatever. And we close the chapter on the strategic importance of re-taking Glogova there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can have the usher assist with moving the ELMO back a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, sure. He's answered the question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see we're trying a bit to shift to see each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, could you answer my question: Was it not in fact easier for the Serbs to go through Glogova to get to -- to go through Glogova to get to Kravica than it was for them to go the way you pointed out by means of the second road by the Drina? Was it not easier for the Serbs to go through Glogova? That is all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if a road is longer but safer, it's better than a shorter, more dangerous road. In the same way, it would have been easier for us to go to Konjevic Polje through Kravica, for example, but we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So your answer remains that Glogova was simply taken to just re-take the village. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And to save people's lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- made that point many a time already, Ms. Richardson, referring to how his co-nationals were encircled at the time and they had to be saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that has a strategic value, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It thank you. I'll move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from we're talking about a war where Glogova was taken by the Serbs in May and then re-taken and taken again and re-taken again. I mean, it's a war. You're fighting continuously to gain territory or re-gain what you've lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm ready to move on to my second point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I think the witness has assisted us as best he can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. -- Sir, I'd like you to take a look at this video that we're about to play for you. And this is Prosecution's Exhibit 329. This is Mr. Oric, who is seen on the video, as he is discussing the attack on Glogova. If you could just listen and then I will have a series of questions for you on this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] So the General Staff of the 2nd Corps then decided -- once we established communications with them they decided, okay, let it be like that then as long as there is peace in the house. They really were wild in the field. When they said that they wanted to go and take Glogova, there was no one to stand in their way and say: 'No, you can't.' So now we had to find a solution, how to go into the village and how to keep it. This time we found out that the Chetniks were preparing a strong offensive which would be carried out against the area of Konjevic Polje and Cerska. This was one more reason for us to go into Glogova. And we knew that this road was extremely important to Kravica. We knew that be doing this we would physically cut them off from -- we would cut the road and would physically cut them off from Bratunac. The other thing was -- the other thing was that Glogova was in the shape of a horseshoe and was surrounded on the other side by Chetniks, except for the one side at the bottom which was open. But in this way also, this would mean that Kravica itself would find itself in -- surrounded in the shape of an S; that is, there would be on the one side Glogova, and then a little lower down from the other side, Konjevic Polje. So in this way it would end up in a kind of sandwich between Muslim forces. "And then when -- when the fighters of Glogova went into the village, when they took their trenches, there was -- there was very heavy fighting and quite a lot of Chetniks were killed. The people from Glogova, because they knew their parts, they knew the area so very well, went behind their backs during the course of the night and attacked them in the very early morning. And the majority of Chetniks who were holding this line, protecting the road, were killed. I don't know the exact number, but it was quite a lot. At that time, when the people of Glogova are in their village, I had the task with my little group -- I and my small group at this time had the task of holding the point, the peak, at Lemesac, this is L-e-m-e-s-a-c, which is opposite and faces another peak or another point called Paici, P-a-i-c-i, which was held by the Chetniks. "We had the task of, firstly, blocking off this road to the Chetniks and of keeping -- and of keeping it open for our forces to move along and keeping the Chetniks from there that they would link up with their forces on the next peak which was called Magasici, that's M-a-g-a-s-i-c-i. This was a small hamlet of Kravica. It was just -- there were just four or five Serbian houses on this part, and there were a few Muslim houses as well I don't know exactly how many. But there were no Muslims nor Serbs there. So this was -- that means that this was just a point and it was a strictly military place. From this point, you could control the whole road from Bratunac to Kravica. And as this particular action was not a very big one, there were only -- the only people involved were fighters from the Potocari Territorial Defence, so a team -- so a team of Senad Golubovic's, that is from the Pale Territorial Defence, went up to Magasici. And so -- and so he went there, to Magasici, and then I went with my small team. Our task then was to take Lemesac. Lemesac was not covered by the Chetnik lines, but we thought that if the people from Glogova would go down into their village that the Chetniks would then take this point to cover the village, because if these two peaks, Lemesac and Magasici, were connected, then nobody could be able to use the road between them. And we had to first of all take Magasici and then hold these two points at all costs."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, having heard what Naser Oric has said about his involvement in the Glogova attack, do you still maintain that there was no assistance to the fighting men -- the men who fought under Ejub Golic during this period of time and during this attack?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't like this. I don't agree with this. I don't know who Naser got information from, who gave him information. But I didn't know what TO Potocari even was for a long time and who they were. I don't agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you -- excuse me for interrupting. But if I hadn't seen him around there ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps you can assist us with the map and point out those areas that are located, the ones that Naser Oric is talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment; sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Richardson, it's not our fault. I just don't understand the answer that the witness -- it's an incomplete one in any case for that matter. Let me tell you -- excuse me for interrupting. "But if I hadn't seen him around there ..." And that's all I have in the transcript. What were you about to say or what did you say, if anything, that did not show up in the transcript? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't see him and I didn't hear that he participated on that day anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I thank you for the clarification, and that fills in the blank that there was. Yes, Ms. Richardson, my apologies to you, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, and I do appreciate that, Your Honour, that makes for a clearer record of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you point out for us on Defence Exhibit 793 the area of Lemesac that was just described by Naser Oric where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he can on 7 -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do see it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So perhaps he can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can locate Magasici, and it's right under Magasici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you mark it with a different colour, please. What's the colour used? Because on the monitor it's brown, but I'm sure it isn't brown. So could you underline Lemesac, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you also underline Pajici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already underlined.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you, Your Honour, it is indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could he just point out --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, Your Honour, I have no further questions with respect to this attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But perhaps you can -- you can also point out for us the area of Zagoni on the map if you see it.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you underline it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you or any of the men from Glogova involved in any attacks or counter-offensive in this particular area, the area of Zagoni, in 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay, as far as you know. Okay. Thank you. And I take it that you were not apprised of all the comings and goings of the various men who fought under Ejub Golic during 1992 and the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the men from Glogova and Cizmici, I knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these men that you knew about and you're unable to give a number, were you apprised that they had been participating in attacks in Zagoni, for instance?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it since you were not with your -- I'll rephrase the question. During the period of time that you yourself participated in the attacks, and you stated that you were in the area of Cizmici and Velika Glogova, I take it you were not aware of where the other men were who formed part of the group under Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in Velika Glogova and Vladusici and this forest, those were three groups. I was there in 1992, and this fourth group was in Cizmici. But nobody ever said that they had participated in an attack on Zagoni. I never heard anyone talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But they were -- they would not have told you about this because you were not the leader of that group, would they? They would not have been required to tell you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me personally, but they would have told Ejub and I would know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did Ejub discuss every single attack and every single fighter during 19 -- with you during 1992 and into 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every fighter and every detail, but we talked about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't have any questions with respect to the map at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you to the attack on Kravica which occurred on the 7th of January, 1993. Now, you may have recalled that you testified that you participated in this attack, as did Ejub Golic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in addition to that you also stated that it was - and correct me if I'm wrong of course - was it Ejub Golic's decision to attack Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: On the 3rd or 4th, this was the fiercest offensive and only snow probably saved us from being killed, all of us in Glogova. So we complained and wondered what to do. And he said he had sent help everywhere, to Bljeceva, to Pale, to Suceska, and everywhere else help had been sent. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I imagine, based on what you know, he sent help to these areas such as Suceska and Pale and Potocari because they themselves had a Territorial Defence and had fighters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a discrepancy -- in the transcript it shows as if Ejub had sent help. You've put the question, and probably you're right, that he sent for help. However, I notice Mr. Jones standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's that and it's also there's a double question in there, Territorial Defence and fighters. If the witness answered yes to fighters it would appear that he answered yes to Territorial Defence. So if he could just have one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have a distinction between the two and how you're going to rephrase your question and I also want to make sure that when we have in the transcript lines 11, page 33 and he said he sent help everywhere he meant to say or did say that he sent for help from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And that's what I also said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I understood. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely so, he asked for help from all these places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it to be, but -- and that tallies with your interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please proceed with your question, taking into account the objection that Mr. Jones raised --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which is a valid one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us if the reason that Ejub Golic sent for help to areas such as Suceska and Potocari and Pale was because there was an awareness by Mr. Ejub Golic that there were Territorial Defence men in the area, in those areas?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he knew whether there was any Territorial Defence there, but he asked for help because the Serbs had already taken the left side of the road from Bratunac to Kravica. And we were surrounded again. All of us were there then. We were surrounded again. And I said there were about 2.000 Serbs attacking us at the time. I'd never seen more soldiers in one place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, the reason he sent to Pale, Suceska, and Potocari was because he was aware that there were fighting men, if you can accept this proposition, who would assist.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked for help from those villages. I don't know who was there, but he was asking for help from the villages I listed. And who actually came to help --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: He wasn't asking for help from the civilians of Pale, Suceska, and Potocari, was he?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the fighters. I assume it was fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what sort of help was he seeking?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any kind of help, any kind of help, because we were in danger. And whatever help arrived was welcome, whether it was fighters or food.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you -- when I say "you" -- I should rephrase it, sir. It was Ejub Golic who decided to attack Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993, the date?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not decide. We didn't know. We requested help for men to be sent to help us at Glogova. We ourselves were surrounded. We were running out of ammunition. People had perhaps several bullets each on them. The situation was difficult. It was the snow that saved then us. I think had it not been for the snow we would have all been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, who decided to attack Kravica on the 7th of January if it wasn't Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- or rather, he requested assistance for us at Glogova. There were heavy attacks coming, and we decided to all just go. It wasn't simply Ejub Golic. It was all of us. It was Bozi -- it was Christmastime and this was the best time to try to drive them back from those positions because they were probably drunk. We believed this was our chance to push them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So a decision was made among all of the men in Ejub Golic's group to attack Kravica on the 7th of January. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we had no intention of attacking Kravica as such; our intention was to push them back from these areas, Brezak, Jezestica, to push them back and stop them from killing our people because this was a situation we no longer put up with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you decided to launch a counter-attack. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, when you said you all decided to go, could you tell us where the other men -- or where perhaps you were when you decided to go into Kravica. What area specifically were you in?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the area of attack or my whereabouts at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll clarify. You stated "we decided to go." Could you tell the Trial Chamber where -- where you were when you decided to go and who were you with when you decided to go.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We took off from Brezak. It's the Muslim village that we left at the time. There were between 40 and 50 of us in the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And why did you take off from Brezak? Who made the decision for you to take off from there?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was where most of the attacks were coming from, the attacks against us, and we can no longer defend ourselves and that's why we went there. The remaining people who were at Glogova were holding other lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what other lines were they holding?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broader lines, Velika Glogova, the entrance to Bratunac on the way into Glogova, and then over in the other area, Halilovici, and Laksici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So only 50 of you decided to go and launch a counter-attack. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we set out from that side. I didn't know if there was anyone else around. Probably other people arrived, probably help arrived. I don't know who exactly arrived, what sort of help, but some help arrived and we set out from there. I was wounded early in the morning at 8.30 and 9.00, and I had no idea what went on from that point on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever it's convenient for you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you -- we proceed, Ms. Richardson, how much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is going beyond all -- all reasonable expectations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I venture to say no more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And re-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Maybe even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there are no substantial issues that I must address, it may be between 20 minutes and half an hour. I'll try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we're talking about another hour at the most with this witness, which will bring us to almost 6.00. Yeah -- next witness is here I take it, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you intend to start with him today, I would imagine? Because if you don't, I mean I'm not going to let this individual stay here waiting -- what time did he get here, do you know? Was he here --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. The witness arrived on Thursday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At 2.00. He's been sitting here waiting since 2.00. This is not fair; I mean, it shouldn't be done this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by the way, this man is ill. He has high blood pressure and blood sugar. Maybe it would be a good idea for him to rest and start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it this way because I feel very strongly about these things and have always felt very strongly on these matters. Usher, could you please ask a member of the Victims and Witnesses Unit to come inside the courtroom so that I speak to -- the representative of the unit only so that I speak to her or him and explain exactly what I need to now. In the meantime, let's continue, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, you were just testifying about the assistance that you received -- well, I don't want to put words in your mouth at this point, so perhaps I can just briefly recap what you've said on the record. You stated that at least 50 of you proceeded and that you went to the counter-attack. And you said that probably others arrived to assist. First, could you tell the Trial Chamber how it was that Ejub Golic sent to these different areas for assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean which manner? In what manner?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In which manner, yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How did he do this?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sent people from Glogova who had no weapons, who were not at the line, at the front line. He sent those people to go and seek help everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And he sent people to -- I take it he didn't send the same person. He sent different individuals to different areas. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Several different people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in addition to Potocari, Suceska, and Pale, he also sent someone to Beleceva [phoen]. Do you recall if he sent someone to Beleceva or Beleseva? I may not be pronouncing it correctly.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bljeceva perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sent someone to there, to Pale, to Suceska, everywhere, to all these places where he believed that people would come and help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. In addition to the ones that you listed, did he send some -- anyone to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. He sent men everywhere to seek help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, it's very important, sir, that you tell us exactly where it was that he sent these individuals. These are very important proceedings and we need to be as specific as possible when we can. So could you answer my question: Did he send anyone to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I think he sent a total of between 10 and 15 people and these people went to different places in these areas and probably they also went to Srebrenica. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they go on foot or did they have another means of transportation such as horses or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment. Let's -- let me have a word with the representative of the VWS. Oh, I didn't mean the head. I didn't mean the head of the unit. I mean, I just meant the lady who is tending to the witness. Madam, my apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAILLOUX
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour, it's okay for me. It's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but I didn't ask you -- last thing I dreamt was to get the head -- That's a small misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Head of the unit. I just want the young lady who is tending to the next witness and not Madam. I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAILLOUX
utterances.text: But it's -- do you prefer that other person? For me it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because this is a rather simple formality that I just want this lady to have a word with the next witness, explain to him the predicament that we are in, and that, if at all, we will only have maybe a maximum of about 20 to, maximum, 30 minutes which we could dedicate for him, if at all, whether he would prefer particularly since he is not the fittest of human beings, whether he would prefer that we sent him back to the hotel now so he rests and then we start with him tomorrow morning. So -- but again, I mean, last thing I expected was to have you involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAILLOUX
utterances.text: It is a pleasure to come to your courtroom. So we will do it straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I just want a sort of reply and then, if he prefers to go to the hotel, I'll just send the witness out for a couple of minutes, I'll get him here, I'll apologise to him, and he can then be escorted to the hotel and I will explain to him exactly what. All right? Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAILLOUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At least it wasn't the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to everyone, and to you particularly, Ms. Richardson, for having interrupted to you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, sir, you said Ejub Golic sent 10 to 15 people to different areas. In your opinion, during the counter-attack while you were present in Kravica, did these other people from the different areas arrive? I can rephrase the question if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll restate my question to you. You said that probably others arrived to assist you and Ejub Golic and the 15 other men when you attacked -- excuse me, a counter-attack on Kravica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these other people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment and one other thing because I think I better do this. And please redact this position -- this part from line 20 -- sorry, from line 12 of page 42 until line 23. The reason -- let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. Again, sorry, but it was important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, we were discussing the assistance that you received from the different areas. You stated that Ejub Golic had sent to different areas about 10 to 15 people to ask for assistance. Now, my question to you is: You stated that "probably others arrived." I'm just quoting what you stated. Could you tell us whether in fact it's your belief and understanding that these others who arrived came from the areas that Ejub Golic sought assistance from?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say "probably others arrived," were you present when they arrived, others who were not part of the four groups of men led by Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's why I'm saying that I'm merely assuming. I didn't see any of those men. It was early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, did you later hear or did anyone tell you that assistance did come, as Ejub Golic had sought?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the fighting began, the firing was heavy, the fighting was heavy. So I assumed that help had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did Ejub Golic, as far as you know, tell the different -- tell the 10 to 15 men to communicate to the areas such as Potocari, Suceska, and Pale, to tell them that he was planning the attack for January 7th?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He sought help for us, the people of Glogova, not for an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, when you say he sought help, what kind of help were you -- was he seeking as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any help, both in terms of manpower and in terms of ammunition. Any help was welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But the help was so that -- to assist with your counter-attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no intention of attacking Kravica. That is the truth. We had no such intention. Our intention was to push them back from those areas, Brezak, and those areas just to relieve our own situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So the other people who arrived to help you from the different areas -- you say probably when others arrived the fighting was fierce. Is it your position that they never knew what day the attack in Kravica was supposed to take place, that Ejub Golic never told them?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did. I think, by some logic, we assumed that the easiest for us to push them back would be on the 7th because that was the Orthodox Christmas, it fell on that day, and we reckoned this was our opportunity to push them back from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the other groups who -- who you said are -- that -- the help that you -- that arrived, is it your opinion that it was just coincidence that they, too, arrived on the 7th and assisted on the attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I can't say whether it was the 3rd or the 4th of January, but he sent those people out, he did. Now, I can't say whether this was a coincidence or whether it happened for a reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you, sir, that it was not a coincidence, that this -- that the attack on Kravica was planned for the 7th along with Ejub Golic, his group, and from fighters in the areas that you just suggested -- that you just testified Ejub Golic sought assistance from. Those groups were Suceska, Pale, Potocari. Can you accept that position?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like a video to be shown to the witness, and this is Prosecution's Exhibit 329. And the time is 3.23.19.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Naturally we had a meeting of the War Presidency, meetings of the subregions, that is the complement that we had before, the president of the subregion was Hamed Salihovic. And the decision was reached that it had to be taken at all costs. Immediately the plans started to be worked on. As far as regards reconnaissance, it wasn't necessary to carry out reconnaissance because everybody knew exactly where the lines were and where it could be attacked -- where the attacks would come from -- would be carried out. We observed them for days, but we just didn't have the means to attack them. We watched every move of theirs and every change along their front lines. So they -- so they did the plan very -- very quickly, Hamed Salihovic and Ramiz Becirovic. "This wasn't any particular plan that you had to be very clever about. It was just a question of allocating directions and lines of attack along the firing lines, on the front lines. As the people from Glogova had already gone into Glogova and cut off that road and were -- and were doing very well to keep the barricades they had established along the road toward Bratunac. "Ejub said that he didn't need very many extra men to cover these -- these lines, that he needed just two anti-aircraft machine-guns on two points and not -- or several machine-guns which would have enough ammunition, that they would be able to shoot as much as they needed to if the Chetniks were to attack, but that this whole line around the other side would move towards Magasici and -- that is, along this line from Magasici, Gavrici, and Tursan Brdo. So he would go with his people from Glogova together with the Pale Territorial Defence. They would attack from this flank and Konjevic Polje. As Konjevic Polje zone of responsibility extended immediately to -- right up to, rather, Kravica, but they would deploy their forces so that they could attack from the other flank. The Potocari Territorial Defence, the Kragljivoda Territorial Defence, and Suceska Territorial Defence would carry out ground forces and would act from the direction of Susnjari, from the direction of Pale, and the direction of Jaglici."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, having listened to Naser Oric discuss the participation of the various Territorial Defence unit from Suceska, Pale, and others, is it still your position that the attack on Kravica was not a planned one, the attack that occurred on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in fairness to the witness the date of 7th of January was not mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The date has not been mentioned. In fact, I thought this whole process was to establish actually whether the arrival of all these forces from everywhere on the same -- at the same time -- that's what I was expecting from the video recording actually, the decision to attack on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's why I allowed the objection before he gives the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll come back to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So rephrase your question on --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because of course you have every right to ask the question at this stage that you intended to ask at this stage but without reference to the 7th of January because, as Mr. Jones pointed out, that was not mentioned as--

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Leaving aside the 7th of January, having heard of the involvement of at least Ejub Golic, is it still your position that there was no planning on the part of anyone outside of Ejub Golic's group to attack on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, we've come back to the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour -- to attack in early January, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Even that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but even that. I mean, here we are talking of -- forget the fact that you know exactly the entire content of this interview and that we also know it and that Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic know it as well, but the witness doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it has to -- the question that you have to put to the witness has to be a neutral one without any reference to any particular day. The interview here refers to an attack, a planned attack, on Kravica. It doesn't specify when. So stick to that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll -- that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you want to tie it up to a particular date, you are perfectly entitled to do that later. But not at the present moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Having heard Naser Oric, sir, in this video, including what he has said about the involvement of Ejub Golic, is it still your position that there was no planned attack for Kravica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ever?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Glogova and the attack on the Muslims of Glogova, I believe there was no plan from Glogova. We only asked for help -- to be helped. I don't know what information he had or what they were doing up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the -- what took place in Kravica on the 7th, now leaving aside the video, and the fierce fighting that took place, did Ejub Golic recover - and I say Ejub Golic along with his men - recover any type of weapons in that action?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness was not getting interpretation. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's important to know. Have you heard the question that Madam Richardson put to you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you need -- thank you for pointing that out, Ms. Vidovic. Please, Ms. Richardson, you need to repeat the question and I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation. I told you in the beginning last week that if at any time you are not receiving interpretation to draw our attention straight away because we are not in a position to know because we are following in English, not in Serbo-Croat. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to say it right away, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. It's -- yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Regarding the attack on Glogova -- Kravica on the 7th of January, and you indicated previously that there was fierce fighting that day. Do you recall whether Ejub Golic and the men associated in his group recovered any weapons that day?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in the morning at around 8.30 or 9.00 I was seriously wounded at Brezak. I was transferred to Cizmici and from there to Srebrenica, and I spent three weeks in hospital in Srebrenica. So I'm not familiar with anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But you don't discount the possibility that weapons were recovered, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what, do you -- where does it take you if it is a -- discount the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he doesn't know, that's it. I mean, it's -- try to establish --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you ever told that weapons were recovered in Kravica by Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I didn't know. Maybe some infantry weapons, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll move on to another area. Were you aware of whether or not Ejub Golic and his men had taken part in an attack or a counter-attack in the area of Glodjansko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What hill?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. -- Usually Mr. Di Fazio performs better than you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can spell it out for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he can help us --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if his pronunciation would be better but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please spell it out. Spell it out, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's best we spell out for the record, in any event. The name of the area is G-l-o-d-a-n-s-k-o [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Glodjansko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now what you said, but, no, no, it's not familiar, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of whether or not Ejub Golic and men from his group participated in any type of attack or counter-attack in this area?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be shown a video at this time. And again, that's Prosecution's Exhibit 329.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "Daniel PERRY: Surprise attack on Glodjansko Brdo. When you attacked the trenches, it's a surprise attack. Is that correct? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, we surprised them. "Daniel PERRY: "When the attack occurs, you're very close to the enemy because you have to sneak up. Is that correct? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "Daniel PERRY: "The attack takes place over a period of how many hours? How long does it take to actually have the trench line? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] It took a long time. I don't know how many hours. "Daniel PERRY: How long would you say? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly. "Daniel PERRY: You were at the battle, though? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Yes. When you go into something like that, you lose all sense of time and place. "Daniel PERRY: So it could have taken a short period of time then? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't a short time. They offered great resistance. It wasn't -- it wasn't just -- it wasn't just bang, bang, and they run away, and then let's go on. They have rifles and ammunition. "Daniel PERRY: They offer enough resistance that Mr. Golic is coming up with his troops on the flank and behind. So that they are now -- if they are offering so much resistance they are sitting in there between you and Mr. Golic and having to retreat down the back of the hill? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Who? Who now? "Daniel PERRY: Who? The Serb soldiers? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] They could have gone in that direction. I can show you on the map. Can I have the map? "Daniel PERRY: Certainly. What you're saying, though, is that the resistance lasted a long period of time while they were in the trenches? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "Daniel PERRY: Okay. And what I'm saying to you is Mr. Golic, according to what you've explained, is coming up to the flank and in behind -- if you can, if they're still sitting in the trenches and they're offering resistance to you and your units were coming up facing them, then what is happening to the Serb soldiers at that point? "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you now. If I'm -- if I'm attacking here from the front, a frontal attack, I can guarantee that the line is at least 2 kilometres -- at the very least 2 kilometres long and it's a very broken line -- "Daniel PERRY: Except for a line that long, you have to have a lot of Chetniks on that line. "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] Look now. If Ejub attacks from this side and he destroys this trench at the beginning, he surprises them and destroys it, that means that they have now discovered it, but then there's a second trench which covers this first one and can immediately start shooting. So the first trench is eliminated, but you can't get to the second trench because they've now opened part of it there towards the first trench. Let's -- let's just say for the sake of argument that Ejub Golic was able to get around the back of the first trench and to destroy it, but all of the others still had a chance to leave. "Daniel PERRY: Yes. But at the same time he -- don't forget that Ejub Golic is still moving. "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] But it's not just that he's going. They're shooting."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, having watched this portion of the videotape and a description of Ejub Golic's participation by Naser Oric on the attack on Glodjansko Brdo if I'm pronouncing it correctly, do you have any knowledge of this attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a misinterpretation of what was seen in the video. Naser Oric was not describing anything that had to do with Ejub Golic. It was rather the investigator who insisted that Naser Oric describe this, and Naser Oric is providing a hypothetical account of events. So it can't be put to the witness that this is how Naser Oric described Ejub Golic's participation in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't disagree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Respectfully, all of it -- let's assume for argument's sake that this is what was happening -- this is what happened. This is the gist of the statement being made allegedly by Mr. Oric here in this tape --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, my question to the witness is simply whether or not he has knowledge of Mr. Golic's involvement in Glodjansko Brdo, having heard what he's heard on the videotape, whether it's a hypothetical or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically he didn't even have to hear the -- what there was on the tape in any case. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So having heard what was said on the tape, does this jog your memory or does this give you a better recollection or is your answer still you're not aware of Ejub Golic's involvement in Glodjansko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he participated with anyone in Glodjansko Brdo, and I don't know where Naser got this information. I can't say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Thank you. Now, I just have a few more questions for you. You were asked about Ejub Golic and whether or not you were aware of his position in the Bratunac municipality. Do you recall that? In 1993.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, were you -- when you were in Srebrenica after you were injured, and I believe you went back to Cizmici, but you returned to Srebrenica in March of 1993 and you stayed in Srebrenica until the fall of Srebrenica with the exception of going to visit your mother in Cizmici. I believe that was your testimony. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spent about three weeks in hospital and then I didn't get to Srebrenica as soon as UNPROFOR arrived. It was sometime in the summer of 1993 that I went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall during that period of time while you were in Srebrenica whether your -- your -- excuse me. I'll rephrase the question. During the time that you were in Srebrenica, were you aware of any problems involving men who were under the command of Ejub Golic? When I say "problems," that they had been involved in any crimes or had been arrested in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know of someone by the name of Nezir Mrdzic, M-r-d-z-i-c.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nezir Mrdzic, Kezo, yes, I do know him. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he was one of the men who fought under Ejub Golic, who had Ejub Golic as his leader?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall sometime in 1994 that he had been arrested and was being held in Srebrenica prison?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall that your -- that -- I'll rephrase the question. What was he arrested for?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He created a problem. This Nezir Mrdzic, known as Kezo, and as far as I know Ejub locked him up in prison. He personally locked him up in prison. The man was in prison for two or three months. Nothing was solved. He didn't get any decision from anyone, and I remember that Ejub -- he was probably drunk. I wasn't there in that group, but I heard that he was a drunk. And as nothing had been resolved he set out to free him from prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Who set out to free him from prison?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ejub set out with a few men. I don't know who exactly was with him because I wasn't there, but that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how did they set out to free him? Did they go to the prison and release him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as a result was Ejub himself either arrested or any type of legal action taken against him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
