utterances.text: I'm not aware whether or not he was arrested. I know that he did get Kezo out of prison and that he personally took him back to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "personally took him back to prison," on whose orders did he take him back to prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why? Because you're assuming that he did this under orders?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why did he take him back -- first he frees him and then he takes him back. Why did he take him back to prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for two or three months this man had been sitting in prison, and his case did not proceed. He didn't get any kind of decision, any kind of sentence or anything. And then one evening he got drunk and set out toward the prison and freed him from the prison. Probably when he had sobered up and realised what had happened, he took him back again. And then the authorities, I don't know who was involved, they speeded up the proceedings in Nezir's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In addition to that incident involving Ejub Golic, do you know if he was involved in any other criminal activity or was he arrested or accused of committing any crimes in Srebrenica in 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. Criminal activities is a very broad idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question and be more specific. Were you aware that Ejub Golic had been accused of killing two Muslims in Srebrenica in 1994?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was he ever arrested for killing these two Muslims?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't arrested. I think that the men around him would not have allowed his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "not allowed," what do you mean by that? Not allowed the police to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wouldn't have let the police arrest him and there would probably have been a clash between his men and the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know whether during that period of time he was under the command of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who would have arrested him in Srebrenica during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could have arrested him, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No. You stated that he would not -- his men would not have permitted his arrest. So I'm asking: Who would have arrested him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was in a position to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Who was in a position -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think anyone could have arrested him because the fact that he wasn't arrested shows that nobody could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Kezo was arrested. Who arrested Kezo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ejub arrested him, put him in prison, got him out of prison, and then put him back again. It was Ejub who did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time I would like the witness to be shown an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please bring your cross-examination -- because -- to an end because we can't continue like this and we're going to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, this has gone beyond all acceptable limits. And we will stick -- and I'll discuss this with my two colleagues tomorrow. Once you indicate how much time you're going to spend with each witness, that will be the maximum time that you will be allowed, Defence and Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of fact I am not going to show the witness any exhibits at the moment. What I will do, however, is ask him -- I'm bringing my examination to an end. We do have some documents here; however, I'll put those to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's simply this, that I'm not sure if we exceeded any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not referring to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just your indication that we'll be subjected to the same rigid scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be asked to stick to the time limit that you indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just clear we're being punished for the Prosecution's failure to stick to their time limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everyone will be asked to that. It's a simple of -- we have to regulate our -- discipline ourselves. We can't go on like this. At 10 -- quarter to 5.00 you said you needed 20 minutes, maximum 30. We lost a couple of minutes because of the other matter that we dealt with, but I went through the transcript. At 4.50 you started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're 30, 40 minutes already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I have exceeded my time and so I will proceed to ask a couple of questions and end my cross-examination. However, I will introduce this new document through this witness. The ERN number 02622014 and the next document is 0622015 [sic]. And I will not belabour the documents before this witness, except with respect to document ERN 02622014.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to bring your attention to a portion of this document towards the end which starts with -- it's the last sentence on the document. And just to put the title of the document into the record. "Army of Republika Bosnia and Herzegovina, 2nd Corps command, security department, Tuzla, dated the 8th of March, 1995, Tuzla." It is entitled "Ejub Golic, violent behaviour." And it also states towards the end of the document: "Immediately on this case to the 2nd Corps military security service bodies, take all legal measure for the people who were taken out of prison to be returned and to take legal measures against Ejub Golic for the committed -- for committed criminal acts." Now, you've already testified that you were not aware of any action being taken against him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. All right. Now, I would put the -- thank you. I would put the second document before you and that's ending 2015. Now, this document is dated the 11th of March, 1995. It is from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, transitory municipal council Srebrenica. And the second page of this document -- and I'm referring to the English version, page 2. I am going to read from a portion of the document. "Full support was given to our commander of the 28th Division, Brigadier Naser Oric; "Decision was brought on imprisoning and taking Nezir Merdzic and Sadik Begic to the municipal prison, which was already done;" Towards the end it states: "On the issue of the perpetrator of the harsh incident, Ejub Golic, the proposal of our Commander Brigadier Naser Oric was adopted, that he, taking into consideration the difficult situation we found ourselves in consults you gentleman, which he already did with his letter from 10 March, 1995 ... We ask you to adopt the proposal of our Commander so that the Golic -- so that the case "Golic" leaves the least possible consequences for all of us in the region of Srebrenica municipality free territory. "At the same time" -- the last sentence, "the same time, we ask you again that as soon as circumstances are created, you allow our Commander Brigadier Naser Oric to continue his planned journey, since it is of great importance ..." Now, my question to you, sir, is whether or not you were aware that Naser Oric had been informed of Ejub Golic and the incident of him taking men out of the prison in Srebrenica. Were you aware that Naser Oric had been apprised of this?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Naser Oric was in Srebrenica at the time. I don't think he was there. I think he was in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, either the Prosecutor is reading a different document or they are again dealing with an incorrect translation because what she read for the case must be left for some better times. There is nothing that sounds even remotely like it in the document that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the translation is being challenged here --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure exactly what part of the translation is being challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But the document I have -- I'm reading from the English version. So in any event, Your Honour, we'd like these two documents to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the first one -- yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the penultimate portion, 02622015, that's the document we're talking about. I'm talking about the second-to-last section that was quoted by the Prosecutor, but the quote was not consistent with anything in the Bosnian original. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can resolve this matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, please do. We are not going to deal with it now. The first of these two documents with ERN 02622014 consisting of one page in the Serbo-Croat language and two pages in English is being entered in the records as Prosecution Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P577, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 577. And the subsequent document with ERN 02622015 consisting also on one page in B/C/S and two pages in English is being marked as Prosecution Exhibit P578. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you just stated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more, Ms. Richardson, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two questions and one exhibit. As a matter of fact, I can make that one question and one exhibit, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hold you responsible if this man has to stay here another day because I will give Ms. Vidovic all the time she requires to conduct her re-examination and there -- we also need time to put questions ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the -- that the witness be shown a new exhibit, and this will take exactly no time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, registrar, please prepare me for tomorrow, to your leisure and pleasure, a time -- an indication of how long this witness has been testifying, leaving out, of course, interruptions, particularly -- I mean -- particularly on the Prosecution's side, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- sir, just so that you're aware, I just have one question with respect to the documents that I'm about to show you. It has to do with whether or not you receive any commendation or whether your name had been submitted for any commendation or special declaration by Srebrenica, the armed forces in Srebrenica. So that is the -- that is exactly what my question will deal with. Now, the first document, this is a document ending in ERN number 00717689. Now, the English of that document has -- has -- has also been handed out. And I should say this is just the relevant pages of this document that pertains specifically to this witness, and it's from the Army of the Republic of BiH, the 28th Division command, Srebrenica, the 3rd -- April 3rd, 1995. And it has your name, (redacted), and I'll direct you to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Richardson. I have to do another redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prepare it please, Madam Registrar. And while being prepared -- also while the original document, in other words the B/C/S version will be filed regularly, the English translation thereof will go under seal. Yes, let's get it over and done with, Ms. Richardson, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I referred you to ERN number 00717692. That's where your name appears on the B/C/S version of the document. Now we're looking at the English version that says page 1 of 3, and this is just an excerpt from that document. And, sir, it has your name. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Witness, do you know who Azmir Golic is or was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was or who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the lad. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is he also from Glogova and he was one of the members of Ejub Golic's group?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the first -- with respect to the information regarding yourself -- and I don't have the time to read the entire portion of this document, but it does state that on the 9th of May, 1992, with a group of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session again, because then, if you're going to read and the document is public, in public domain, one can trace who the individual is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This document also states with respect to this individual, "he was a native -- when the war broke out he was in his native Glogova, and after Glogova had been occupied by the aggressor with a group of Territorial Defence members he went to Cizmici via Stolac on the 10th of May, 1992, and put himself at the disposal of the Srebrenica TO." Now, sir, having heard that information about this individual, is it in fact true that he also put himself at the disposal of the Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That also was out of place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That also is out of place because you don't have a recognition or an admission from the witness that anyone else put himself at the disposal of the Srebrenica TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Golic, as far as you know, not you, as mayor, as Mayor Golic referred to in this document put himself at the Srebrenica TO -- at the disposal of the Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in Velika Glogova with the same group that I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And finally with respect to the last document that's been put before you, and that's ERN number DA183832. I believe you have it. Now, this document is from the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 2nd Command, Department of Morale, and it's dated January 17, 1995, information, your proposal for assimilating measures and awarding declarations. Strictly confidential, et cetera. The following decision has been made. And I'm reading from the document. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That your name, sir, is listed here as one of the individuals who is -- a decision has been made regarding receipt of a decoration. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see my name in this document, but I never heard that I was proposed by anyone for this decoration, nor was I ever in fact awarded a Gold Lily.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to add something in relation to what we said about what I was looking at a while ago. Another document that I -- that had my name on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. If you would allow the witness to add anything. That's why -- I don't have any more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you want to add? Please be as concise because otherwise you're going to stay here another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll tend to these documents and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then let's redact these last three lines that the witness pronounced, please -- stated. The first of these documents with ERN 00717689 to 708, both pages included, is being marked as Prosecution Exhibit P579. The corresponding translation into English consisting of three pages will be kept under seal. The second of these documents with ERN DA18-3832, two pages in the Bosnian language, will be marked as Prosecution Exhibit P580, and a corresponding translation into English and consisting in two pages will be kept under seal. Yes, Madam Vidovic, I -- I wouldn't even dare tell you finish by a certain time, given these circumstances. But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we could just go into private session for a while, I wish to deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the last document that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You tell us the corresponding page in English. We can perhaps arrange to have it on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course, Your Honour. The page is 25 in the English and 50 in the Bosnian. 25 for English, 50 for Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it reads here, I quote the beginning: "The largest Bosnian village in Bratunac municipality, Glogova, was the one that suffered the worst genocide." Have you found that? That is in the bottom third of the page on page 50. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please listen closely to what I'm reading. "The original deadline for the surrender of arms set for the 20th of April, 1992, was extended until the 27th of April, 1992, because of problems in Potocari, and the SDS had enough time to plan their raid on Glogova." Please, Witness, do you remember yourself testifying about these events surrounding the collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if this is in fact true at all, what the book states, that a collection was scheduled for the 24th and then postponed until the 27th, or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was never postponed. The date was the 25th, the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This date, the 24th of April, 1992. You said the 25th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he said the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say, Witness? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mispronounced. I meant April. I may have said "May," but what I meant was April.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, what was the date of the ultimatum, once again?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: April or May?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this date, the 20th of April, 1992, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I don't know who wrote this book. It's not correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember on the first day of your testimony I asked you about the dreadful scene you saw, the dead body of Mustafa Ibisevic and those of his sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm referring to transcript page 11940, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, look at what it says here in this book. Look at page 51. That's the next page, the very beginning of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 25 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the first sentence. "The most dramatic scene of this horror was when Muharem Ibisevic who had been captured stood between his sons Mujo and Mustafa, embraced them, and courageously together with his son awaited for death. The inhabitants of Glogova buried the father and his sons in the same grave without separating the father's hands from the shoulders of his sons." Did you testify here about Mustafa Ibisevic or Muharem Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Ibisevic was the father of Muharem and Mujo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, is it correct to say that Muhamed [as interpreted] Ibisevic stood between his sons or was that a completely different person, Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa was their father.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So is what this book says correct about these people?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to gain time I referred to D742, the list of missing and killed in Glogova, where you can see that Mustafa Ibisevic with his sons Muharem and Mujo was killed, and what it says in this book does not correspond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is what this book says correct, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And also specifically in connection with this, it says here that you buried these people with arms around each other.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did bury them in the same grave; there was only one grave for all three of them. But we couldn't bury them in an embracing position; we had to separate them otherwise the grave would have had to be wider.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the grave like?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to Muslim custom, there is a grave and we put them in.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So is what the book says about this true?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, if you recall, asked you a number of questions about your training in the anti-sabotage platoon. I refer to page 11956 of the transcript, lines 7 to 14. And you gave certain replies. When asked about the anti-sabotage platoon when you described your experiences there, were you referring to experiences in the JNA or to experiences in the war?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to my experience from the JNA, the former army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you were asked a number of questions that had to do with reporting on what the men who went to observe the Serb lines and positions transmitted. The Prosecutor used the expression "your smaller groups reported," in the plural, "to Ejub Golic." Can you explain to Their Honours whether this was simply a conversation or whether it was a kind of formal reporting, for example, the submission of written or oral reports?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was written. It was just a formal [as interpreted] conversation. I know that we didn't have any paper. They would just come to see him and they would tell him those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. It says in the transcript it was a formal conversation, but you explained that nothing was written down. Did you say "informal" or "formal"?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people who were reconnoitring would come and say what had happened, what they had seen and heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people duty-bound to come and give this information or could they have not turned up or said anything?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not duty-bound to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, while you were either in Velika Glogova, as you described, or in Cizmici, were any written reports compiled about events and activities in Glogova before the entrance of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the men outside Golic's group, members of other groups, have any information about what you in Glogova were doing in combat with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question isn't quite clear to me. What men are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you said that you did not write any written reports to anyone outside your group or in your group. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Other men in other groups, whether they were in Bljeceva or Potocari or Srebrenica, to the best of your knowledge, did they have any information about what you were doing in your combat activities against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody sent any information about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else now. You were asked something about the 24th of December, 1992. The Prosecutor asked you how 150 armed men managed to defeat a strong Serb army including air force and artillery. Is it correct that in the early morning of the 24th of December, 1992, you only managed to break through the Serb line in a certain area and reach your group in Velika Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We managed to drive away those men, and later on that day there were planes and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would the usher please show the witness a new document issued by the command of the Drina Corps. The number is 04268489. This is a combat report of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, on the 25th of December, 1992, and I will quote. "In the afternoon of the 24th of December, 1992, the enemy in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade carried out intensive combat operations on the Kravica-Magasici axis and captured the village of Glogova (formally a Muslim village). However, in the morning of the 25th of December, 1992, due to strong resistance put up by our forces, these operations became less intensive." And then if you look where it says under 2, "our forces," it says: "Forces of the Bratunac Brigade with a backing of the command corps managed to partially consolidate their ranks and halt an enemy attack with artillery and air support. During the afternoon hours of the 25th of December, 1992, they succeeded in retrieving a lost part of the terrain that the enemy had captured." Witness, is this what you were trying to explain in your responses to questions put by the Prosecutor, that you managed to break through the line and hold it, but that later that day you were attacked by all kinds of means by the Serbs? Does this reflect the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this number would be Defence Exhibit D788?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D813, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D813, so this document with ERN 04268489 to 490 with the corresponding English translation is being marked Exhibit D813.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you something about the interviews shown to you by the Prosecutor, parts of the interview of Naser Oric. You saw an interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at present I don't have -- I'm not sure whether it's P329 and the time 3.23.27 --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, let me remind you, that's the part of the interview in which Naser Oric mentions Glogova. Do you remember the first clip that you were shown today of the interview?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From what you saw today, is it clear what date Naser Oric is talking about?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the 24th of December, 1992? The 1st of January? The 2nd of January? The 3rd of January? The 4th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only objection is that at this point we are still on re-direct and I suggest that non-leading questions should be put and this is far beyond an open-ended question in accordance with re-direct procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was: From what you saw today is it clear what date Naser Oric is talking about? This was the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, but then Madam Vidovic proceeded to put a number of dates as an option for him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but those are -- doesn't change anything. The substance of the question remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's to illustrate a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's not waste time or lose time on this any further. Please, Ms. Vidovic -- I would like Ms. Vidovic not to go beyond the 6.30 limit. Otherwise, if that is not possible, I am not going to stop you, then he has to return tomorrow. And we need to --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honour. Let me just put two or three more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in connection with this did you ever hear, you personally, did you ever have any information that Naser or anyone from Potocari was at Lemesac?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about any possible tasks of any groups that may have been there?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor dwelt for a long time on the 24th of December, 1992, and put several questions to you in connection with the strategic importance of Glogova on the 24th of December, 1992. You persistently responded that you were trying to help people. For you, the people from Glogova, was there a greater strategic interest than to save the lives of the thousand or so people who were encircled in Velika Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in our interest to save the lives of people; it wasn't any kind of strategic interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When arriving at the decision to go and help them, did you bear in mind the massacre of the 9th of May, 1992, that had taken place in Glogova? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course we were because what happened to those people was the same thing that happened later on on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. As regards the 24th of December, 1992, the Prosecutor tried to show you a part of the war diary and quoted an excerpt --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can quote it without showing it to the witness, because everybody heard it. It says here: "The attack on Glogova was planned for the 24th of December, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anywhere who planned that attack?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From what was read out to you, was it clear to you who might have planned the attack from that sentence read out to you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody planned the attack. The situation in Glogova was what it was, and when Ejub told us -- and he said, What shall we do? Shall we go there or let the people be killed? We decided to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you need -- I'm speaking to the -- about the 24th of December, not the 29th of December, 1992, when, as I said, you were totally encircled. I'm talking about the 24th of December. Did you then need weapons or did you need men?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We needed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will put one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Ejub Golic in the course of 1992 to the best of your knowledge at any time have the position of deputy commander of the Bljeceva company?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was he ever part of the Bljeceva company?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and I certainly appreciate your high sense of cooperation. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You mentioned the force of Nurif Hasanovic's men. Did they stay in the area of Srebrenica later on? You only mentioned that they participated in one attack. Did they stay in the area or did they go back to Tuzla? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, about 20 men, remained in Cizmici. The others went with Nurif. He said at the time, at least, that he was headed for Konjevic Polje, but I have no idea where he ended up. All he said at the time was that he was headed for Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions. First of all, when Ejub Golic sent out some men to ask for help, have you been present when he did send out these people?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't present. I arrived later. The situation was difficult for us in those days. We were looking for a way out. So he said to the people who were assembled there, he said that he would send his men out to get help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to answer the question and just the question. The question was whether you were present or not. So, it just requires a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise you are going to stay here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Were you -- when you mentioned that he sent out, that what you have heard from others -- but you have not present when Ejub Golic sent out certain people to certain villages?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when he sent these people out, but I did hear later on that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And when he heard from him later on, did he tell you to whom he would send his men? Would he just say, Send somebody to Suceska or Magasici or Potocari and say, or would say, He sent them to certain people in these villages?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention any specific men. He said that he had sent men to those areas, to those villages, to seek help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you have been in hospital in Srebrenica you told us that a nurse mentioned to you this man was Naser Oric. Now, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, how often would you see -- this man who has been either indicated to you as Naser Oric, how often did you see him in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just that once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... time now. And you had also mentioned that other people would come to the hospital. There have been quite a few people, you have told us, who came around. Yes?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the wounded, that there were quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: You told -- in your testimony you said there were people coming in and out at all the time. So besides Naser Oric, there had also been people coming in and out. Did they come in your room as well?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who were with Naser at the time were in the room. I was running a high fever and my wound was beginning to rot, but the people that I was talking about originally were the wounded. Those were the people I had in mind when I talked about the coming and going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So your testimony: There were people coming in and out all the time and that you thought that Naser Oric was an ordinary person like anyone else. So it appears as if Naser Oric was not different from other people who came to the hospital. Is that a correct conclusion which I draw?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him then. There was some people with him, I don't know who exactly, and the nurse told me, That's Naser Oric. I mean, my own situation was difficult. Those people kept coming and going. I meant the wounded. There were a great number of those coming in from all over the place. Those were the people I meant. Those who were less seriously wounded would just go, and those who were more seriously wounded would be taken in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you have been there about three weeks you told us and with four other men. And how long have you been together with the same people? A day or a week or so? Was there a change every day or have you been together with certain people for some time?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the same people would stay for a five- or seven-day period. That's what I think, but I was suffering from a very high fever at the time and there was precious little medication. Therefore, I was not entirely conscious during this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But you have been in this very bad situation for the whole three weeks?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not throughout, but the best part, yes. My wound was beginning to teem with maggots and there was no medication to be used. They could no longer dress my wound, so I had to go as quickly as possible. There was no food left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But even if you have been in a bad situation but over such a long time and other people having been with you in the same room for a couple of days, wouldn't there be an occasion to talk with them about events which happened in the area?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember talking about to anyone about these things. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So you would have been silent for all three weeks or is that your --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I kept silent. I was in so much pain that I was unable to think about anything else. I wasn't thinking about asking questions about other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's just that the witness previously when asked about this had given the answer that he hadn't -- "I had my own problems. I expected my arm to be cut off then my body temperature was very high every day." I don't know where Your Honour was leading to with that question, but it seems that you failed to take into account that this was a man who was on the -- with extremely serious health problems. I'm aware Your Honour is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I really want to say something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, you don't need to explain. I think, leave it at that. Judge Brydensholt has another final question. I am not going to put any questions so that we can send the witness home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you left the hospital in order to come home, as you explained, in what way did you do that? You were seriously hurt, I understand. Had you any way of transport, or how?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no means of transportation. One of my brothers came to visit who was at Cizmici. My mother kept a cow at Cizmici, so that's where I had went in order to be fed and try to improve my health situation. So I left with my brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But how did you go there?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: On foot. He helped me along. He held my arm. We took a long time getting there, one whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I will not ask you any questions, even though I had intended to. This brings your testimony to an end, sir. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher, but before you leave the courtroom I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and myself for having been kind enough to come over and give testimony and also wait here over the weekend because we had not finished with your testimony in time. I can assure you that you will be given all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. And before you leave again, once more, on behalf of everyone here I wish you -- I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to thank the -- all the staff for having bore with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow, Mr. Jones, I would like some information about whether the tests that are going to be carried out by the gentlemen you mentioned in the motion involves any chemical examination or chemical treatment of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we can revert to you on that. I'll allow my colleague to respond because she's more familiar with the techniques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but not now. Tomorrow. I'm not going to keep anyone else --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was simply to say that I assume we can let you know tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And give as much details as possible, so that we can possibly hand down the decision tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of October, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.30 p.m.,
